summary: This informational memo from Ascend specifies a tunnel management protocol that lets remote dial-in users reach their home network as if directly attached to it. It documents a vendor protocol and is not an Internet standard.

eli5.summary: A secret tunnel from your hotel room straight into your own house, so you feel at home.

questions: what is the ascend tunnel management protocol
how do remote users access home networks
subtitle: A tunnel protocol for remote dial-in users to reach their home network.

tldr.problem: Remote dial-in users need to appear as if they are directly connected to their home network, even though they are connecting through a Network Access Server on a remote network.
tldr.mechanism: ATMP establishes a tunnel between a Foreign Agent (the NAS) and a Home Agent (on the home network) using shared-secret authentication, encapsulating traffic with GRE and a tunnel ID.
tldr.outcome: Remote users can use home network addresses and access both IP and IPX traffic as if physically present, though this is a vendor-specific protocol that did not become an Internet standard.

facts.label: Authentication method
facts.value: MD5 hash of authenticator and shared secret

today: RFC 2107 is an Informational document describing a vendor-specific protocol from Ascend Communications. It was not adopted as an Internet standard; the IETF developed Mobile IP and other standard mobility protocols instead. The protocol is described here for historical reference and because it influenced later tunnel management thinking.

sections.title: The Tunnel Vision Problem
sections.content:
Ascend Tunnel Management Protocol (ATMP) solves a mobility problem: when a remote user dials into a Network Access Server, they need to appear to have a home network address, not an address from the remote network. The RFC specifies how a Foreign Agent (the NAS) and a Home Agent (on the home network) set up a secure tunnel to carry this traffic.

ATMP assumes a simple model: one user stays connected to one NAS for the duration of their session. Unlike Mobile IP, which allows a mobile node to roam between foreign agents while keeping the same address, ATMP is designed for dial-in scenarios where the connection is more stable. The protocol supports both IP and IPX traffic, allowing users to run protocols beyond just TCP/IP.
sections.eli5: When you call your office from the road, a tunnel carries all your data to your home office network so you look like you're at your desk.

sections.title: The Three-Way Handshake
sections.content:
ATMP uses three key entities: the Mobile Node (the remote user's client), the Foreign Agent (the NAS it connects to), and the Home Agent (on the home network). The client is unaware of ATMP; it simply uses standard PPP and believes it has a home network address.

The FA and HA perform a registration dance. First, the FA sends a Registration Request with the user's home address. The HA replies with a Challenge Request containing a randomly generated 16-octet Authenticator value. The FA computes an MD5 hash of this Authenticator plus a shared secret, and returns it in a Challenge Reply. The HA verifies the hash matches (proving the FA knows the shared secret), then issues a Registration Reply with a unique Tunnel ID that identifies this session's tunnel.

Once registered, all traffic from the mobile node is encapsulated by the FA in GRE packets, carrying the Tunnel ID in the GRE Key field. The HA decapsulates and routes these packets according to a Connection Profile, which specifies how to forward traffic for this user. When the user disconnects, the FA issues a Deregistration Request to close the tunnel.
sections.eli5: The office and the hotel work out a secret password, verify each other knows it, then set up a tunnel with a unique ID so the office knows which guest's traffic is which.

sections.title: The Protocol Messages
sections.content:
ATMP defines seven message types, all sent over UDP port 5150. Every message starts with a Version field (always 1), a Type field, and a 16-bit Identifier to match requests and replies.

Registration Request (Type 1) contains the Foreign Agent's IP address, the Mobile Node's home address and netmask, optional IPX network and station numbers, and the name of a Connection Profile to use for routing. Challenge Request (Type 2) carries a 16-octet Authenticator (or a Result Code if an error occurred). Challenge Reply (Type 3) returns the MD5 digest of the Authenticator plus shared secret. Registration Reply (Type 4) includes a Result Code and a Tunnel ID if successful.

When the session ends, the FA sends a Deregistration Request (Type 5) with the Tunnel ID. The HA responds with a Deregistration Reply (Type 6). If either agent detects a problem (such as an unexpected reply), it sends an Error Notification (Type 7) with a Result Code and Tunnel ID. Result Codes indicate success, authentication failure, resource exhaustion, parameter errors, invalid Tunnel IDs, timeouts, network unreachability, or general errors.
sections.eli5: Seven types of messages pass between the office and hotel: a registration request, a challenge, a response to the challenge, a confirmation, and later a deregistration and its response, plus error messages if anything goes wrong.

sections.title: Authentication and Trust
sections.content:
ATMP protects the registration phase using a Challenge-Response mechanism similar to CHAP (Challenge Handshake Authentication Protocol). The Home Agent issues a random challenge; only a Foreign Agent that possesses the shared secret can correctly compute the MD5 response. The HA verifies the response and accepts the registration only if it matches.

This mechanism authenticates the Foreign Agent, preventing unauthorized agents from establishing tunnels. However, once registered and a Tunnel ID is issued, the actual data packets encapsulated in GRE are not individually authenticated by ATMP; security of the tunnel depends on the GRE encapsulation and physical network security. The shared secret must be securely configured on both the FA and HA out of band, and the UDP checksum must be computed and verified on all messages.

The RFC notes that configuration information—including the Home Agent address, shared secret, and Connection Profile name—is typically delivered via RADIUS (Remote Authentication Dial In User Service), as shown in an appendix. This allows centralized management of tunnel parameters without hardcoding them in each NAS.
sections.eli5: The secret password proves the hotel knows who it is before the office opens the tunnel. After that, trust is maintained by the fact that data is wrapped in a secure envelope and physical network security.
